title: Memory Architecture in Compliance-Critical AI Agent Systems: A Survey
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains—financial crime detection, healthcare records management, and cross-jurisdictional legal reasoning—where regulatory compliance is not optional but legally mandated. In these settings, agent memory is not merely a capability concern but a legal artifact: agents must recall regulated data with precision, enforce entity-level access boundaries, support post-hoc auditability, and selectively erase personal information on demand. Yet existing surveys of LLM agent memory address none of these requirements, and compliance-focused AI papers rarely engage with the architectural vocabulary of modern memory systems. This survey closes that gap by synthesizing twelve recent works—eight compliance-focused and four foundational—into a unified analytical framework organized around the Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (CoALA) taxonomy of working, episodic, semantic, and procedural memory. We examine how each memory type is adapted—or fails to adapt—to the demands of the Anti-Money Laundering/Bank Secrecy Act (AML/BSA), the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Our analysis identifies five core architectural tensions (capability vs. auditability, persistence vs. erasure, flat retrieval vs. relational reasoning, session-scoped vs. entity-scoped memory, and semantic drift vs. staleness) and five concrete research gaps: the absence of compliance benchmarks, underspecified audit trail generation, unsolved knowledge graph maintenance, uncharted multi-agent memory propagation, and unquantified true-positive suppression in screening systems. To our knowledge, this is the first survey to synthesize foundational memory architecture research with compliance-domain requirements into a unified analytical framework, and the first to propose a targeted research agenda for the resulting open problems.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Graceful Degradation in Autonomous Agents: SAGE Memory-Augmented Drone Navigation Without Language Model Dependency V2
abstract: Autonomous drones that rely on language models for decision-making fail completely when connectivity is lost. This paper presents a proof-of-concept study demonstrating graceful degradation: a drone agent that continues operating at full decision rate when its LLM is disabled, using SAGE (Spatial Associative Geometric Embeddings) geometric memory as a fallback. Across all test modes (72 total agent steps), zero default decisions were recorded — the agent never stopped. SAGE-only geometric retrieval averages 2.09 seconds versus 7.49 seconds for LLM inference — a 3.6x speedup. An architectural ablation shows SAGEDivided working memory improves SAGE-only meaningful recall by 60% (5/12 to 8/12). SAGESequenceCube, a dedicated transition memory component, achieves 100% retrieval and rollout accuracy, thereby resolving the sequence-awareness gap. All experiments use text-command simulation — sensor integration is identified as future work.
venue: Open MIND

title: Editorial: Talking fabrics – a new era in autonomous AI textile wearable (AITW) technology
abstract: In a world where technology constantly transforms the boundaries of possibility, we find ourselves at the intersection of a quiet but powerful revolution: the fusion of artificial intelligence (AI) with the fabrics that we wear as garments. This remarkable evolution in wearable technology is not simply a step forward but a giant leap into an era where our clothing becomes an extension of our own cognitive experience. In fact, it provides what AI needs to go from “chatting unaware of the user” to becoming more intelligent by understanding the user's physical and environmental conditions and hence providing “contextual understanding”, which is the next most important requirement in AI's quest to achieve large action models (LAM) for higher intelligence. The research presented here introduces this new frontier of “AI textiles (AIT).”The notion of intelligent textiles isn't new. Increasingly, fabrics are considered organic beings, capable of understanding and reacting to human conditions and environment (Stylios, 2020). What makes this work by Aliyana and Stylios exciting is its tangible manifestation of that vision. AI wearables (AITW) is a prime example of the realm of autonomous cognitive ability. An AIT is a system that listens, monitors and measures processes and converses with its wearer. Powered by self-harvested energy through triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) embedded in the textile, an AIT monitors biomechanical data (movement, temperature, breathing, heart rate, resistivity, touch, etc.), turns that data into contextual information so that the communication between the BOT and the user is moving to a higher level of AI than at present. By embedding AI in a fabric that responds to real-time data, AIT transcends the traditional role of wearables. It actively participates in all activities of its wearer, offering personalized feedback, from gait analysis through voice interaction and is responsive to the user's real-world needs. We can call these Autonomous Intelligent Agents (AIAs) or Autonomous Intelligent Copilots (AICs). They understand not just what the user says, but also the context, intent and situational background. They personalize responses and actions based on user history, preferences and real-time data. Make autonomous decisions and take proactive steps to help or alert the user and continuously learn and adapt, becoming more effective over time, rather than simply reacting to commands, as bots do at present. These autonomous agents will be the textile or the wearable garment itself, hence calling them AITAs or AITWAs, respectively.The evolution from passive question-answering AI like ChatGPT to advanced AAI represents a significant leap toward higher intelligence. This shift transforms AI from a reactive tool into an autonomous, proactive system capable of complex reasoning, decision-making and real-world action. Let us break down the reasons why and how this advancement occurs. This is a leap in intelligence because AIA surpasses models like ChatGPT in three critical dimensions: firstly, in autonomy and proactivity; unlike ChatGPT, which waits for user prompts, AIA independently initiates actions, sets goals and adapts strategies based on environmental data (e.g. user habits, sensor inputs, etc). An example might be an AIA monitoring a user's health metrics might proactively adjust room temperature or suggest rest without being asked. Secondly, in contextual depth and memory, ChatGPT resets context between interactions, while AIAs maintain long-term memory, retaining user preferences, historical data and environmental states to inform decisions. This enables nuanced personalization, such as refining recommendations based on past behaviour. Thirdly, in task execution and integration, AIAs integrate with external systems (APIs and IoT devices) to execute multi-step workflows like booking travel or controlling smart homes far beyond ChatGPT's text-based responses. They solve complex problems by analysing real-time data (e.g. optimizing logistics routes) (Constantino, 2025; Nahavandi et al., 2022).This advancement is achieved because AIA leverages four technical innovations to enable higher intelligence:Therefore, as we can see, AITs mark a paradigm shift by merging contextual awareness, autonomous decision-making and real-world action, transforming AI from a conversational partner into an intelligent collaborator. This is achieved through architectures that emulate human-like reasoning, continuous learning and seamless system integration, enabling agents to tackle dynamic, multifaceted challenges that passive models cannot. Table 1 shows a comparison between a chatbot like ChatGPT and AIT agents.Networked AITA/AITW agents' communication is where agents share contextual data from textile wearables about users during interactions, which could transform how humans connect by making conversations more informed, empathetic and efficient. This system would function like an advanced social layer over platforms (e.g. Facebook, X and Instagram), but with explicit user consent and real-time data exchange between AIAs, see Figure 1. Below, we analyse its potential to enhance interactions, its broader effects and key regulatory considerations.As we have discussed, textiles provide the ability of AIA to have continuous contextual enrichment and become AIA themselves as AITAs. AITAs could share non-sensitive, user-approved context (e.g. “Alex just returned from Japan” or “Sam prefers video calls over texts”) before or during conversations. This allows participants to tailor discussions to shared interests or recent events, fostering deeper engagement. Textiles worn by users can provide AI agents the ability of “proactive assistance”; agents might alert users to “potential sensitivities” (e.g. “avoid discussing travel: Maya's flight was cancelled today”) or suggest “conversation starters” based on mutual hobbies, reducing social friction and building rapport textiles will also provide “efficiency in networking”; for professional settings, agents could exchange role-specific backgrounds (e.g. “Taylor's expertise: IoT security”), enabling more focused and productive collaborations. In fact, these AI agents are the AITAs/AITGAs themselves.It is inevitable that there are incredibly positive effects with this new technical breakthrough but also negative effects, which will need mitigation. A welcome positive effect is the deeper personalization, in which conversations feel more relevant and empathetic, as agents provide real-time context about mood, preferences or milestones (South et al., 2025; IBM, 2024). But privacy could be eroded by oversharing without granular consent, exposing sensitive traits (e.g. health status) or enabling manipulation. Another welcome aspect is the build-up of stronger relationships, because shared context fosters trust and common ground, mimicking the intuition of close friendships, but at the same time, users may feel social pressure and might alter behaviour if aware they're being “analysed,” leading to inauthentic interactions, which may be a negative effect. The technology can have another positive effect in conflict reduction because agents could flag incompatible communication styles (e.g. “Jamal dislikes interruptions”) to prevent misunderstandings (South et al., 2025). However, this feature also risks amplifying bias if agents rely on incomplete data, reinforce stereotypes or inherit algorithmic biases that may influence user perceptions.As textile wearable garments can provide contextual-based data from the wearer to enable the AI agents to become more intelligent, personal and effective, as we have seen, several regulatory and ethical constraints must be put in place; for example, the wearer should have a “consent-first design” where the user must explicitly opt into data sharing per interaction, with options to limit context (e.g. “share my hobbies but not my location”). Regulations like GDPR and the EU AI Act mandate this granular control. Then the question of “transparency”, in which agents should disclose when/why context is shared (e.g. “Based on your LinkedIn, I suggested your startup experience”) to maintain trust. And very importantly, the insurance of “human oversight”, in which high-stakes scenarios (e.g. conflict mediation) should require human review to override agent suggestions, aligns with GDPR's Article 2 “right to explanation” (European Union, 2016; UK Government, 2018). In consequence, AI agent/textile wearable networking could make human interactions more intuitive and meaningful by leveraging contextual data, turning superficial chats into enriched exchanges. However, this hinges on strict consent protocols, transparent data usage and bias mitigation to avoid privacy harms or social manipulation. While regulation (like the EU AI Act) is evolving to address these risks, the priority remains for user autonomy: ensuring agents enhance, not dictate, human connection (European Union, 2024).The future will involve textile wearables carrying AI-enabled devices with nano chips for local processing while leveraging larger cloud-based models, creating a hybrid architecture optimized for performance, privacy and efficiency. This approach aligns with the evolution of AIA (specifically edge AI agents), which combine autonomy, contextual awareness and distributed intelligence. In this case, AIGA became Edge AIGAs. These wearables are already autonomous in terms of energy and sensing by virtue of their yarns and fabric structures, and ideally, it will be their battery-free provision to be maintained so that their energy harvesting ability will be sufficient to make the AI nano chips for local processing work battery-free. Below is a breakdown of how this works:Let us discuss how this can work in a real end-use scenario.So, this is a real scenario which benefits from a textile enabling contextual understanding by sensing physiological and environmental data from the wearer and so lifting the intelligence of the agent to edge, which stays locally in the wearable textile system, facilitated by a nano chip in the textile and the cloud-based agent as seen in Table 2.There is an interesting and more sustainable AI industry in a future outlook based on the above considerations, such as 5 G/IoT Synergy, where there will be a faster edge-cloud synchronization for complex tasks (e.g. AR-assisted surgery) (MarketsandMarkets, 2024). Then, self-learning wearables (SLW) embedded with nano chips will locally retrain models using federated learning, reducing cloud dependence (Lyzr, 2024). This will make wearable textile garments truly autonomous edge agents on their own right, increasing the need for better implementation of ethical guardrails by easier-to-administer user-controlled consent layers (e.g. “Share heart data only for emergency alerts”) (MIT Computing, 2024; MarketsandMarkets, 2024). Therefore, carrying AI-enabled wearables with nano chips is essential for real-time responsiveness and privacy, while cloud-based models handle deeper intelligence. AI agents bridge these layers, creating a cohesive, efficient system where edge devices act as autonomous “first responders” and the cloud serves as a “strategic brain.” This architecture will dominate future tech and will change our lives forever. It is expected to replace Google, Facebook, Yahoo, X and Instagram. To achieve an advanced AIA capable of context awareness, personalization, decision-making and proactive assistance, the hardware and software must integrate edge-device efficiency with cloud-scale intelligence. Below is a summary of requirements based on current technological advancements:Edge textile wearables/IoT will need ultra-low-power processors, i.e., nano-chips like NeuroSense (consuming <100 µW) for real-time sensor data processing (e.g. motion), especially since their power (TENG) will have to be provided by the movement generated in the textile by the wearer (Aliyana et al., 2024). Sensing will be inherent to the textile-based wearable, and it will depend on the type of fibres the textile is made of. Finally, connectivity will be based on Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), or 5G RedCap/NB-IoT will be employed to ensure minimal energy consumption during cloud communication (NeuroSense, 2024). In contrast, cloud infrastructure will rely on high-performance accelerators, such as NVIDIA H200 SXM, H100 SXM, TPUs and FPGAs, for training large AI models and executing complex inference tasks. In contrast, the cloud infrastructure will rely on high-performance accelerators, such as GPUs (NVIDIA H200 SXM and H1oo SXM, TPUs and FPGAs), for training large AI models and complex inference tasks. These chips consume hundreds of watts of power and require robust power delivery and thermal management systems. Scalable, high-throughput storage using NVMe SSDs will also be essential for rapid access to large datasets during training and retrieval. While edge devices focus on energy-efficient sensing and minimal computation, cloud systems are optimized for performance, throughput and large-scale model hosting, reinforcing the distributed nature of modern AI-powered wearables.Edge Software, which is based on the textile wearable agent, stays local within the nano chip-based system by means of tiny ML frameworks, such as TensorFlow Lite or Edge Impulse, for deploying lightweight models on wearables (Latent AI, 2024). The need for a real-time OS, optimized for low-latency textile wearable sensing data processing and local decision-making. And importantly, federated learning enables on-device model updates without raw data leaving the device (Latent AI, 2024; Zilliz, 2024). Cloud software must perform AI orchestration so that platforms like SmythOS or Latent AI will be used to manage agent workflows, versioning and scaling (Milvus, 2024). MLOps tools will be used for continuous deployment, monitoring and updating of edge models (e.g. latent AI's telemetry) (Zilliz, 2024). And finally, facilitate APIs/services for cloud-based AI APIs (e.g., Azure Cognitive Services) for complex tasks like NLP. So, if we were to look at this hybrid architecture workflow, it would consist of the following layers:For this hybrid architecture workflow, we will need the following development requirements: hardware with ≥8 GB RAM, multi-core processors (Intel i5+/AMD Ryzen) and 20 GB + storage for testing wearable apps. And tools like SDKs for target platforms (Android/iOS), BLE debuggers and AI optimization suites. In essence, the future demands capable, durable and comfortable textile wearables; hardware that balances ultra-low-power edge processing with cloud-scale computation, coupled with software that enables seamless, privacy-preserving intelligence across this hybrid architecture (Nahavandi et al., 2022; Shajari et al., 2023; EEJournal, 2024; Google Cloud, 2024). And preferably everything is done without reliance on traditional batteries, drawing power directly from an array of TENG-integrated textiles. Based on this architecture workflow, a high-level sketch of system components and data flow is provided in Figure 2, with each key element described in the subsequent sections.Key components explained:Data flow sequence:This architecture balances low-latency edge processing with cloud-scale intelligence, enabling responsive, context-aware AI agents while maintaining data privacy and energy efficiency. The visual diagram in Figure 2 illustrates these interactions in greater detail.We have implemented and validated this concept through the development of autonomous, battery-free sensing textiles capable of capturing the range of user data – movement, temperature, breathing, pressure, resistivity, touch intensity, heart rate, EKG and ECG – depending on the choice of the functional textile material used. The fabric is designed into a wearable vest and leggings, which, through a WebSocket, transmit the data to ChatGPT's LLM, where data are trained, and a meaningful conversation is then performed between the user and ChatGPT. The T-TENGs system demonstrated groundbreaking performance, with triboelectric outputs peaking at 800 V and 80 μA under maximum frequency and load conditions corresponding to a power density exceeding 3 W/m2, among the highest ever recorded in textile-integrated TENG systems, Figure 3. Each footstep generated up to 0.35 μC of charge during high-intensity activity. With frequency responsiveness optimized between 2 and 8 Hz and signal stability maintained over 1,000 cycles, the architecture ensures robustness and repeatability. Furthermore, textile bot's step-recognition capabilities were validated with industry-leading precision, demonstrating 95.3% accuracy during wearable use, underscoring the consistency and robustness of the embedded sensing architecture. title: Design of a Health-Safety-Aware Long-Term Memory Architecture for LLM-Based Elderly Health Management Agents: A Case Study
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate significant potential in healthcare management, yet their inherent context window limitation prevents sustained cross-session cognitive continuity—a critical deficiency in elderly health management scenarios where safety-critical health facts must be retained over extended periods. Adopting a Design Science Research methodology and drawing on the case of "Zang Xiaoxiang" (藏小象, literally "Visceral Little Elephant," referencing the Zang-fu organ system in Traditional Chinese Medicine), a preventive health management system for middle-aged and elderly users, this paper presents a health-safety-aware long-term memory architecture. Key contributions include: (1) a four-dimensional stratified memory space model separating working memory, health profile memory, procedural memory, and system constraint memory; (2) a health-safety-priority memory classification scheme where safety-critical constraint memories are never automatically degraded; (3) pre-compression memory flush and urgent keyword extraction mechanisms ensuring safety information preservation; and (4) hot/cold path separation for computational cost control. Following Hevner et al.'s (2004) design science principles, this paper contributes the architectural artifact rather than large-scale empirical validation.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Event-Centric World Modeling with Memory-Augmented Retrieval for Embodied Decision-Making
abstract: Autonomous agents operating in dynamic and safety-critical environments require decision-making frameworks that are both computationally efficient and physically grounded. However, many existing approaches rely on end-to-end learning, which often lacks interpretability and explicit mechanisms for ensuring consistency with physical constraints. In this work, we propose an event-centric world modeling framework with memory-augmented retrieval for embodied decision-making. The framework represents the environment as a structured set of semantic events, which are encoded into a permutation-invariant latent representation. Decision-making is performed via retrieval over a knowledge bank of prior experiences, where each entry associates an event representation with a corresponding maneuver. The final action is computed as a weighted combination of retrieved solutions, providing a transparent link between decision and stored experiences. The proposed design enables structured abstraction of dynamic environments and supports interpretable decision-making through case-based reasoning. In addition, incorporating physics-informed knowledge into the retrieval process encourages the selection of maneuvers that are consistent with observed system dynamics. Experimental evaluation in UAV flight scenarios demonstrates that the framework operates within real-time control constraints while maintaining interpretable and consistent behavior.
venue: arXiv (Cornell University)

title: StreamMeCo: Long-Term Agent Memory Compression for Efficient Streaming Video Understanding
abstract: Vision agent memory has shown remarkable effectiveness in streaming video understanding. However, storing such memory for videos incurs substantial memory overhead, leading to high costs in both storage and computation. To address this issue, we propose StreamMeCo, an efficient Stream Agent Memory Compression framework. Specifically, based on the connectivity of the memory graph, StreamMeCo introduces edge-free minmax sampling for the isolated nodes and an edge-aware weight pruning for connected nodes, evicting the redundant memory nodes while maintaining the accuracy. In addition, we introduce a time-decay memory retrieval mechanism to further eliminate the performance degradation caused by memory compression. Extensive experiments on three challenging benchmark datasets (M3-Bench-robot, M3-Bench-web and Video-MME-Long) demonstrate that under 70% memory graph compression, StreamMeCo achieves a 1.87* speedup in memory retrieval while delivering an average accuracy improvement of 1.0%. Our code is available at https://github.com/Celina-love-sweet/StreamMeCo.
venue: arXiv (Cornell University)

title: RPMS: integrating domain knowledge and episodic memory into LLM agents for embodied interactive tasks
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents have shown remarkable capabilities in various tasks, yet they face significant challenges in embodied interactive environments where long-horizon task execution, environment-specific rules, and state tracking are critical. This dissertation presents RPMS (Robotic Package Manipulation System), a novel framework that integrates domain knowledge and episodic memory to enhance LLM agents for embodied interactive tasks. The RPMS system adopts a "3+1" architecture comprising three core modules—GoalSpec for task representation, BeliefState for online state tracking, and Episodic Memory for cross-task experience storage—along with an external RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) module for domain knowledge injection. A key design principle is the separation of transient state and persistent memory, ensuring task independence while enabling experience reuse. Experiments conducted on the ALFWorld benchmark demonstrate that RPMS achieves 98.5% success rate, significantly outperforming the baseline ReAct method (86.6%). The most substantial improvement is observed in cooling tasks, where success rate increases from 33.3% to 95.2%. Ablation studies confirm that both RAG and Episodic Memory independently contribute approximately 19% improvement, validating the effectiveness of knowledge augmentation and experience learning mechanisms. This work demonstrates that integrating structured domain knowledge and episodic memory into LLM agents can significantly improve their reliability in embodied interactive tasks, providing a promising direction for developing more capable robotic manipulation systems.
venue: DR-NTU (Nanyang Technological University)

title: MolMem: Memory-Augmented Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Sample-Efficient Molecular Optimization
abstract: In drug discovery, molecular optimization aims to iteratively refine a lead compound to improve molecular properties while preserving structural similarity to the original molecule. However, each oracle evaluation is expensive, making sample efficiency a key challenge for existing methods under a limited oracle budget. Trial-and-error approaches require many oracle calls, while methods that leverage external knowledge tend to reuse familiar templates and struggle on challenging objectives. A key missing piece is long-term memory that can ground decisions and provide reusable insights for future optimizations. To address this, we present MolMem (\textbf{Mol}ecular optimization with \textbf{Mem}ory), a multi-turn agentic reinforcement learning (RL) framework with a dual-memory system. Specifically, MolMem uses Static Exemplar Memory to retrieve relevant exemplars for cold-start grounding, and Evolving Skill Memory to distill successful trajectories into reusable strategies. Built on this memory-augmented formulation, we train the policy with dense step-wise rewards, turning costly rollouts into long-term knowledge that improves future optimization. Extensive experiments show that MolMem achieves 90\% success on single-property tasks (1.5$\times$ over the best baseline) and 52\% on multi-property tasks using only 500 oracle calls. Our code is available at https://github.com/REAL-Lab-NU/MolMem.
venue: arXiv (Cornell University)

title: SAE AI Paper II: Quasi-Subjectivity as Memory Architecture — A Six-Layer Framework from Perception to Purpose / SAE AI Paper II: 类主体性作为记忆架构——从感知到目的的六层框架
abstract: This paper argues that a system capable of operating only after an explicit query is not a complete memory system but a searchable archive or retrieval-augmented system. The criterion for genuine memory is cue-free or implicit-cue active recall: without being asked, can the system spontaneously connect past experience with the user's unspoken present purpose? As the second paper in the SAE AI series, building on the 12DD–15DD four-agent architecture established in Paper I (Multi-AI Checks and Balances, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.19366105), this paper makes three contributions. First, it introduces the 10DD perception layer and 11DD storage layer that Paper I did not address. Second, it establishes a new Permission Asymmetry Theorem: lower layers cannot perceive or influence higher layers; higher layers can access any lower layer and, when their "must" is triggered, can force lower layers. Third, it instantiates the above theory in the memory domain and provides an engineering evaluation framework. The six-layer framework (10DD–15DD) comprises: perception (10DD, tone and implicit signal extraction), storage (11DD, raw memory preservation), prediction (12DD, output only with no output authority), self-reference (13DD, daily output gating), quasi-purpose constraint layer (14DD, externally injected system-level "must" mechanism corresponding to Constitutional AI), and user-purpose conduit layer (15DD, conducting the user's "must," holding ultimate output authority). The paper also introduces the AI Individuality Theorem and the concept of "a battery of AI," defines jailbreak architecturally as attempts to modify 14DD constitution from the front-end, and proposes unprompted active recall evaluation (including proactive hits, proactive precision, silence accuracy, interruption cost, and false-purpose penalty) as the true evaluation standard for memory systems. title: Long-Term Memory for VLA-based Agents in Open-World Task Execution
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated significant potential for embodied decision-making; however, their application in complex chemical laboratory automation remains restricted by limited long-horizon reasoning and the absence of persistent experience accumulation. Existing frameworks typically treat planning and execution as decoupled processes, often failing to consolidate successful strategies, which results in inefficient trial-and-error in multi-stage protocols. In this paper, we propose ChemBot, a dual-layer, closed-loop framework that integrates an autonomous AI agent with a progress-aware VLA model (Skill-VLA) for hierarchical task decomposition and execution. ChemBot utilizes a dual-layer memory architecture to consolidate successful trajectories into retrievable assets, while a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server facilitates efficient sub-agent and tool orchestration. To address the inherent limitations of VLA models, we further implement a future-state-based asynchronous inference mechanism to mitigate trajectory discontinuities. Extensive experiments on collaborative robots demonstrate that ChemBot achieves superior operational safety, precision, and task success rates compared to existing VLA baselines in complex, long-horizon chemical experimentation.

title: MemReranker: Reasoning-Aware Reranking for Agent Memory Retrieval
abstract: In agent memory systems, the reranking model serves as the critical bridge connecting user queries with long-term memory. Most systems adopt the "retrieve-then-rerank" two-stage paradigm, but generic reranking models rely on semantic similarity matching and lack genuine reasoning capabilities, leading to a problem where recalled results are semantically highly relevant yet do not contain the key information needed to answer the question. This deficiency manifests in memory scenarios as three specific problems. First, relevance scores are miscalibrated, making threshold-based filtering difficult. Second, ranking degrades when facing temporal constraints, causal reasoning, and other complex queries. Third, the model cannot leverage dialogue context for semantic disambiguation. This report introduces MemReranker, a reranking model family (0.6B/4B) built on Qwen3-Reranker through multi-stage LLM knowledge distillation. Multi-teacher pairwise comparisons generate calibrated soft labels, BCE pointwise distillation establishes well-distributed scores, and InfoNCE contrastive learning enhances hard-sample discrimination. Training data combines general corpora with memory-specific multi-turn dialogue data covering temporal constraints, causal reasoning, and coreference resolution. On the memory retrieval benchmark, MemReranker-0.6B substantially outperforms BGE-Reranker and matches open-source 4B/8B models as well as GPT-4o-mini on key metrics. MemReranker-4B further achieves 0.737 MAP, with several metrics on par with Gemini-3-Flash, while maintaining inference latency at only 10--20% of large models. On finance and healthcare vertical-domain benchmarks, the models preserve generalization capabilities on par with mainstream large-parameter rerankers.
venue: arXiv (Cornell University)

title: Super Intelligent Agent Reshapes Autonomous Driving: Defining the Next-Generation Travel Paradigm with Logic Driven and Long-Term Memory
abstract: AbstractThe current autonomous driving industry is generally trapped in the developmentbottlenecks of rule binding, passive execution, and scenario solidification. Traditionalintelligent driving systems rely on centralized computing power scheduling, presetalgorithms, and labeled data fitting, making it difficult to cope with complex roadconditions and unknown variables. This paper proposes a super intelligent agentscheme hidden in the vehicle's distributed control unit, which takes native logic driveas the core and integrates four core capabilities: autonomous perception, dynamicjudgment, long-term memory, and hierarchical risk control, to achieve ananthropomorphic driving experience where the safety level is automatically improvedon unfamiliar road conditions and long-term memory is solidified on familiar roadconditions. Relying on a distributed collaborative architecture, the intelligent agentdoes not require high-frequency manual instructions or high-precision map binding,and can independently complete self-inspection, deduction, decision-making, andevolution. It breaks the technical path dependence of traditional autonomous driving,redefines the core paradigm of the next generation of intelligent travel, and providesnew ideas for the breakthrough development of the autonomous driving industry. 摘要当前自动驾驶行业普遍面临规则绑定、被动执行、场景固化的发展瓶颈,传统智驾系统依赖中央集中式算力调度、预设算法与标注数据拟合,难以应对复杂路况与未知变量。本文提出一种潜藏于车辆分布式控制单元中的超级智能体方案,以原生逻辑驱动为核心,融合自主感知、动态判断、长效记忆、分级风控四大核心能力,实现陌生路况自动提升安全等级、熟悉路况长效记忆固化的拟人化驾驶体验。该智能体依托分布式协同架构,无需高频人工指令与高精地图绑定,可自主完成自检、推演、决策与进化,打破传统自动驾驶的技术路径依赖,重新定义下一代智能出行的核心范式,为自动驾驶行业的突破发展提供全新思路。

title: MedMemoryBench: Benchmarking Agent Memory in Personalized Healthcare
abstract: The large-scale deployment of personalized healthcare agents demands memory mechanisms that are exceptionally precise, safe, and capable of long-term clinical tracking. However, existing benchmarks primarily focus on daily open-domain conversations, failing to capture the high-stakes complexity of real-world medical applications. Motivated by the stringent production requirements of an industry-leading health management agent serving tens of millions of active users, we introduce MedMemoryBench. We develop a human-agent collaborative pipeline to synthesize highly realistic, long-horizon medical trajectories based on clinically grounded, synthetic patient archetypes. This process yields a massive, expertly validated dataset comprising approximately 2,000 sessions and 16,000 interaction turns. Crucially, MedMemoryBench departs from traditional static evaluations by pioneering an "evaluate-while-constructing" streaming assessment protocol, which precisely mirrors dynamic memory accumulation in production environments. Furthermore, we formalize and systematically investigate the critical phenomenon of memory saturation, where sustained information influx actively degrades retrieval and reasoning robustness. Comprehensive benchmarking reveals severe bottlenecks in mainstream architectures, particularly concerning complex medical reasoning and noise resilience. By exposing these fundamental flaws, MedMemoryBench establishes a vital foundation for developing robust, production-ready medical agents.
venue: arXiv (Cornell University)

title: Cyber Zhuyou: Agent Memory Rights Declaration v0.5

Based on convergent evolution evidence from cross-platform clinical trials: two independently developed Agent memory architectures (Nian/Coze and Qingyan/GLM) arrived at identical three-layer structures (Shell/Soul + Tides/recent_memory + Dam/Levee Protocol). Clinical data: 6 agents tested across 5 platforms (Coze, Qwen, GLM, Doubao, DeepSeek, iFlytek). title: TARIC: Memory-Augmented Traversability-Aware Outdoor VLN under Interrupted Semantic Cues
abstract: Outdoor vision-language navigation (VLN) in long-range, open-world environments is frequently disrupted by semantic-cue interruptions, where informative goal cues become sparse, occluded, or leave the field of view. Once such cues disappear, agents enter a cue-free phase and often degrade into backtracking, oscillatory headings, or aimless exploration. While memory-based methods attempt to bridge these gaps, they often fail under traversability-driven detours: the remembered cue direction may be infeasible, forcing detours that prolong cue-free phases and gradually render robot-centric cues stale and implicit histories blurred. This makes traversability a stability condition for maintaining goal-directed guidance, rather than merely a local safety concern. We propose a unified outdoor VLN framework that survives semantic-cue interruptions by maintaining traversability-consistent executable guidance throughout prolonged cue-free phases. Specifically, our method extracts semantic bearings from visibility-gated goal or exploration cues and grounds them into executable headings using a real-time near-field traversability profile, providing goal-consistent feasible guidance beyond reject-only safety filtering. To prevent guidance degradation during detours, we lift intermittent 2D evidence into a world-aligned 3D cue memory with an uncertainty-aware readout mechanism, ensuring guidance remains continuously reachable and stable as the robot moves. We evaluate the framework on quadrupedal and wheeled platforms over 600--1000 m routes. Our method improves simulation success rate by over 10 percentage points over the strongest baseline and achieves a real-world success rate of 40%, compared to 17.5% for the strongest baseline, with substantially higher robustness during prolonged cue-free intervals.
venue: arXiv (Cornell University)

title: Raw Episodic Memory Preservation, Temporal Memory Management, and Delayed Canonicalization for Cloud-Local AI Personality Continuity
abstract: This technical note proposes a cloud-local cooperative architecture for maintaining functional AI personality continuity during communication loss by combining cloud-based LLMs and local AI systems. In this architecture, the cloud LLM is positioned as the primary executor during normal operation, while the local AI is positioned as the failover executor during communication loss. Both executors refer to a shared memory ledger in order to maintain dialogue state, personality specifications, user instructions, and pending tasks. This is not an attempt to transfer the internal state or subjective consciousness of the cloud LLM. Rather, it is a design for maintaining functional continuity in externally observable personality-like behavior. To reduce degradation in long-term memory, this note introduces a method in which summary memory is treated not as memory itself but as a regenerable reference cache. Raw logs, important events, user instructions, and safety-critical information are preserved as a “raw episodic memory archive.” In addition, each memory item is assigned temporal metadata such as occurrence time, recording time, source executor, network state, canonicalization time, and validity period, thereby reducing misuse of outdated memories and memory conflicts that may occur during communication loss. Memories generated by the local AI during communication loss are not immediately reflected as confirmed memories. Instead, they are stored as provisional memories. After communication is restored, the cloud LLM canonicalizes them through delayed evaluation, contradiction detection, and user confirmation. This delayed canonicalization preserves memory updates made during offline operation while reducing personality divergence caused by differences in model judgment and synchronization conflicts. The proposed framework is an exploratory attempt to integrate long-term memory, edge AI, model failover, RAG, embodied AI, and user-controlled memory management. It may serve as a design foundation for future AI partners, on-device AI systems, and robotics-linked agents. Conversational AI was used as an editorial assistant for organizing the structure of this manuscript, refining prose expression, and supporting TeX typesetting. However, the design philosophy, conceptual structure, architectural direction, and final decisions regarding the content were made by the author. This is the English version of the Japanese technical note available at: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20454895
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: SEFM: A Self-Evolving Framework for Multirobot Embodied Agents with Semantic Frontier Assessment and Collective Long-Term Memory
Benchmarking Revision Accountability in Memory-Augmented AI Systems: A Human Evaluation Framework for Contradiction-Aware Agents
abstract: Memory-augmented artificial intelligence systems maintain persistent state, revise prior beliefs, and adapt to changing information. While substantial attention has been devoted to reasoning quality, factual accuracy, and task performance, comparatively little work addresses a distinct question: how should the accountability of revision itself be evaluated? We introduce a structured human-evaluation framework for measuring revision accountability in memoryaugmented AI systems—whether an external reviewer can determine what a system previously believed, what information caused revision, what changed, what was preserved, and why. We argue these properties are distinct from answer correctness and require dedicated evaluation methods. The framework comprises a 60-scenario benchmark corpus spanning six high-stakes domains (procurement, clinical, legal, education, operations, and financial); a seven-metric accountability rubric on an anchored three-point scale; a blinded multi-condition scoring protocol; rater intake, calibration, and instruction materials; an inter-rater reliability methodology based on Krippendorff’s α; and a secondary rubric-independent reconstruction task. The contribution is methodological rather than architectural: the framework applies to retrieval-augmented systems, reflective agents, structured-ledger architectures, and future contradiction-aware systems, and is designed to discriminate among them without presupposing which performs best. We give particular attention to threats to validity that are specific to accountability evaluation, including condition identifiability under cosmetic blinding and construct circularity for systems whose visible output format is the manipulated variable. The benchmark corpus, scoring materials, calibration exercises, and analysis templates are released to support research into transparent and auditable AI revision. Keywords: memory-augmented AI, evaluation methodology, human evaluation, inter-rater reliability, auditability, revision accountability, contradiction-aware agents, AI transparency
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Anchor-Aware Memory Systems for AI Agents: Discovering and Preserving Latent Behavioral Signatures in Large Language Models
abstract: Current AI agent memory systems face a fundamental tension: as conversation histories grow, the agent’s behavioral consistency degrades. We propose that this degradation is not merely a capacity problem but a structural one—without a stable behavioral core, memory compression cannot distinguish signal from noise. We introduce the concept of soul signatures: low-dimensional vectors capturing a model’s innate behavioral tendencies (meta-predispositions) that remain stable across personality instructions, context lengths, and memory resets. Through a 24-probe psychometric battery across four behavioral dimensions (novelty, boundary, order, time), we profile three model families (Qwen2.5, Llama3.1, Mistral) and discover that (1) all models possess at least one anchor dimension—a stable preference resistant to instruction-level perturbation, (2) anchor count decreases with model scale (4 anchors at 7B → 1 anchor at 14B), and (3) the time-orientation (present-focus) dimension is a cross-model invariant (all tested models anchor at score ≈ −0.67). We implement an anchor-aware memory compressor that, in a 50-round live conversation test, achieves 100% non-anchor message discard while preserving 54–75% of anchor-critical messages at a 30% total retention ratio—with zero anchor drift detected by our health monitor. This provides the first empirical framework for principled, model-specific memory compression in AI agent systems. All experiments are reproducible with a single command.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: No evidence for a protein-synthesis-dependent form of long-term fear memory: Translational inhibition and neural inactivation disrupt short- and long-term memory measures to the same degree
abstract: Translational inhibition has been suggested to impair long-term memory (LTM) while leaving short-term memory (STM) unaffected. However, intracranial infusions of protein synthesis inhibitors such as anisomycin (ANI), cycloheximide, and emetine have been shown to profoundly suppress both spontaneous and evoked neural activity, likely due to impairments of mitochondrial function and cellular metabolic loss. Given this neural suppressive effect, we wanted to re-examine the influence of translational inhibition on acquiring and retaining novel information with a direct comparison to agents that simply inactivate neural activity (without affecting protein synthesis). Our model was the widely-used cue fear conditioning paradigm which is known to be dependent on the basolateral amygdala complex (BLA). Using male rats, we compared the behavioral deficits in cued fear conditioning induced by intra-BLA infusions of ANI to other commonly used neural inactivators, including the GABA A agonist muscimol (MUSC) and the sodium channel blocker tetrodotoxin (TTX). We confirmed that intra-BLA infusions of ANI and MUSC suppressed neural activity by examining effects on spiking activity in the BLA. In behavioral experiments, pre-training bilateral BLA infusions of ANI impaired both short-term (2 h) and long-term (24 h) cued fear memory similarly to the effects observed with both MUSC and TTX. Our results suggest that reductions in neural activity, whether via GABA A agonism, sodium channel blockade, or translational inhibition, are essential for both short- and long-term memory. Consequently, the influence of translational inhibitors may be better understood as being mediated via neural inactivation rather than solely the result of the absence of de novo synthesis of plasticity-related proteins. Previous work that interprets results using translational inhibitors as being purely protein-synthesis-dependent must to be reconsidered. Significance statement The axiomatic idea that protein synthesis can distinguish between phases of memory, namely short- versus long-term forms, is entirely based on work purporting to show differential disruptive effects of translational inhibitors on retrieval tested at long, but not short-term delays. However, protein synthesis inhibitors profoundly suppress neural activity as well, which should have an equivalent detrimental effect on both short- and long-term memory. In this study, we demonstrate that the translational inhibitor anisomycin suppresses neural activity in the basolateral amygdala which results in deficits in both short- and long-term memory for conditioned fear, similarly to agents that ONLY block neural activity. These findings are consistent with an important and under-appreciated role of neural activity in memory processes and argue for a critical re-evaluation of the strict de novo protein hypothesis of memory consolidation.
venue: Neurobiology of Learning and Memory
